title: Introduction to the science of language

Language \(≠\) communication
Communication is one of the uses of language but is it really all there is to it?

we can only understand why language is used the way it is only once we know what it looks like

title: Introduction to the science of language
section: Language acquisition as a logical problem: modus ponens
text:
Language acquisition as a logical problem: modus ponens
Premise 1

Syntax is a productive, recursive and infinite system

Premise 2

Infinite rule-based systems cannot be learned

Conclusion

Syntax cannot be learned; ergo the existence of syntax means it must be partly already available to the learner prior to the start of the learning process.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Premise 1


Language is a productive system

any speaker of any language can produce and understand expressions (sentences etc.) that they have never heard before

Language is a recursive system

sentences can contain other sentences

Students attend parties.
I think students attend parties.
You doubt I think students attend parties.
…


Language is an infinite system

what’s the longest sentence?
what’s the biggest number?

title: Introduction to the science of language

Infinite rule-based systems cannot be learned

a baby must transition to an infinite system based on a finite set of data

e.g. establish correspondences between a sentence and a situation it describes

title: Introduction to the science of language

Obvious answer: x = y

Consequently, y = 6

Less obvious answer: [(x − 5) × (x − 4) × (x − 3) × (x − 2) × (x − 1)] + x = y

To learn a rule, the entirety of input is necessary.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Looking for regularities

to describe the structure of an object, we look for regularities
applied to the structure of natural-language objects, this entails looking for grammatical regularities

to establish the relationships between the parts of a whole, these parts must be found and categorised

every natural-language speaker is capable of distinguishing between sequences of symbols/sounds that are a sentence in that language, and those that are not.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Word classes
Word classes (aka ‘parts of speech’) are an attempt at finding regularities in natural-language expressions.

traditional definitions familiar from school are unreliable and circular
instead, formal and distributional criteria are called for

such criteria are deductive in character

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Formal criteria
involve unifying words into classes based on their form, i.e. how they look.

verbs: -ed and its allomorphs
nouns: singular vs. plural forms (glass – glasses; goose – geese)
adjectives: forms of comparison (tall – taller – tallest)

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Distributional criteria
involve unifying words into classes based on their environment.

verbs: cooccurrence with modals (will, must, could, …)
nouns: preceded by determiners/articles (every, the, a)

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Lexical and functional categories
open-class expressions vs. closed-class expressions
Lexical categories possess a relatively obvious descriptive content

nouns (category N) – desk, jacket, solitude, prowess
adjectives (category A) – noticeable, yellow, spicy
verbs (category V) – attend, run, rejoice

Functional categories only carry grammatical meaning

determiners/articles (category D) – the, each
prepositions (category P) – above, in front of, under, behind
complementisers (category C) – that, if, whether

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Phrases
We have seen that

words can be strung together into phrases
those phrases are more than mere sequences of words
one element inside a phrase is always more prominent that all the others
\(\rightarrow\) head
\(\rightarrow\) phrases have internal hierarchical structure

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Dependency grammar
Should be semi-familiar from school (to anyone who went to a Russian school):




pros: good at capturing morphological relations between heads and dependents
cons: not very good at capturing certain other phenomena and relations

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Context free grammars
(formal grammars whose production rules can be applied to a nonterminal symbol regardless of its context): A \(\rightarrow\) α.
S \(\rightarrow\) NP VP
VP \(\rightarrow\) V NP PP
etc.
in linguistics, also known as phrase-structure grammars
pros: captures the idea of lego-blocks familiar from before
cons: too unrestricted (e.g., allows rules like NP \(\rightarrow\) VP PP)

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Yes/no-questions in English
Guiding principle: choose simplest hypothesis consistent with data (aka Occam’s razor).
Initial assumption: tabula rasa; no structure
Data point 1

Dave can’t eat chocolate covered almonds.
Can’t Dave eat chocolate covered almonds?

Hypothesis 1

To form a yes/no question, move the 2nd word to the front of the sentence.

Can this rule be induced on the basis of the available evidence alone?
In other words, does the learner have all the available information to make this generalisation?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Phrase boundaries
How do we know that a certain sequence of words is a phrase, a constituent?

by applying constituency diagnostics

How do we represent the structure of phrases/constituents?

square brackets; syntactic trees

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Constituent structure
How do we know if a string’s a constituent?

if it can be shown to behave as a unit
available tests:

substitution
movement
substitution + movement
ellipsis
clefting

positive result? \(\rightarrow\) we’re likely seeing a constituent
negative result? \(\rightarrow\) inconclusive, let’s use another test

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
In search of constituents: substitution
Can the string be replaced by a proform?

John hit [ the dog with a hat ] in the garden.

John hit it in the garden.


\(\rightarrow\) the dog with a hat is a constituent

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
In search of constituents: ellipsis
ellipsis effectively amounts to substitution by a zero (unpronounced) proform

John hit [ the dog with a hat ] in the garden…

*and Mary petted ∅ in the living room.


Negative result! We should try another test.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
In search of constituents: movement
Can the string be preposed/fronted?

[ The dog with a hat ] John hit in the garden.

\(\rightarrow\) the dog with a hat is a constituent

title: Introduction to the science of language
section: In search of constituents: substitution + movement
text:
In search of constituents: substitution + movement
Can the string be replaced by a proform and then fronted/preposed?

John hit [ the dog with a hat ] in the garden.

[ Who/what ] did John hit in the garden?


\(\rightarrow\) the dog with a hat is a constituent

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
In search of constituents: clefting
Can the string appear inside the It is/was X that P?

John hit [ the dog with a hat ] in the garden.

It was [ the dog with a hat ] that John hit in the garden.


\(\rightarrow\) the dog with a hat is a constituent

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
In search of constituents: summary

available tests:

substitution
movement
substitution + movement
ellipsis
clefting

positive result? \(\rightarrow\) we’re likely seeing a constituent
negative result? \(\rightarrow\) inconclusive, let’s use another test

Asymmetries between words

words form phrases
one element inside a phrase is always more prominent than the others
\(\rightarrow\) head
\(\rightarrow\) phrases have internal structure

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
This is all very, very impressive!

Especially because it all seems to have been learned exclusively on the basis of data.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Properties of syntactic heads

the head bears the central semantic information in the phrase
the word class of the head determines the word class of the entire phrase

if the head of a phrase is N, then the phrase is a Noun Phrase, or NP
similarly for VP, AP, AdvP, PP etc.

heads are normally obligatory, while other material in a phrase may be optional
heads select dependent phrases of a particular word class

these phrases are sometimes obligatory, and are known as complements

He was reading a book.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Unboundedness in questions
One clause boundary:

He said [ (that) he was reading a book].
What did he say [ (that) he was reading __ ]?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
But!
Sometimes wh-questions just seem impossible:


He made the claim [ that he has met Wolverine ]
*Who did he make the claim [ that he has met __]?


He mentioned the fact [ that he had run into Magneto ]
*Who did he mention the fact [ that he had run into __]?



Which is particularly striking given the full acceptability of the following:

Who did he claim [ that he has met __ ]?
Who did he mention [ that he had run into __]?

What is happening here?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Ross (1967)
Certain syntactic objects are impenetrable for movement:

complements of nouns
indirect questions
relative clauses
sentential subjects
coordinate structures
adjunct clauses

These have come to be known as islands, or island constraints.
Let’s consider a few of them.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Relative clauses

They met someone [ who knows Benedict Cumberbatch ].
*Which celebrity did they meet someone [ who knows __ ]?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Sentential subjects

[ That they have met Benedict Cumberbatch ] is extremely unlikely.
*Which celebrity is [ that they have met __ ] extremely unlikely?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Coordinate structure
They ordered [ tiramisu and espresso ].

*Which dessert did they order __ and espresso?
*Which beverage did they order tiramisu and __?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Adjunct clause

They ordered tiramisu [ after they had met Benedict Cumberbatch ]
*Who did they order tiramisu [ after they had met __ ]?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Poverty of the stimulus?

island effects (i.e., unacceptability of long-distance dependencies across an island boundary) are robustly attested in all speakers of all languages

clearly an exaggeration but a legitimate one

consequently, they are part and parcel of what a speaker knows (or, rather, of the knowledge of language they possess)
what kind of data are required to arrive at this target state?
what kind of data are available to the learner during acquisition?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Reflexive pronouns
Every speaker of English agrees that

Norbert remembered that Ellen painted a picture of herself
*Norbert remembered that Ellen painted a picture of himself.
Norbert remembered that Ellen was very proud of herself.
*Norbert remembered that Ellen was very proud of himself.


\(\rightarrow\) reflexives (-self-pronouns) take antecedents (i.e., what they denote) in the domain of closest subject

and let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that that information is available to the learner in the data.

even though it actually doesn’t appear to be

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Leddon and Lidz (2006)
Sentences like the above never occur in child-directed speech

10,000 wh-questions in CHILDES database
0 wh-questions involving a wh-expression with a -self-pronoun/personal pronoun/proper name inside it
analogous Google search only returns linguistics articles

Consequently, no data on which to build inductions.

title: Introduction to the science of language
section: List of induction problems so far
text:
List of induction problems so far
We have already seen that we humans are in possession of knowledge that could not have come from primary linguistic data:

syntactic islands
constraints on self-pronouns

Let’s add a couple more.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Induction problem 3: Subcategorisation
The English verbs eat and devour are similar both lexically and grammatically in that both involve the consumption of nutrients:

John eats pizza.
John devours pizza.

Let us assume these observations are available in the input.

Yet, the two verbs are also very different:

John eats.
*John devours.

These facts are a part of every English speaker’s knowledge of language.
Can a language-technology AI system (such as ChatGPT) capture this distributional pattern?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Induction problem 4: that-trace effect
Big subordinate clauses: that and tense on verb

We think [ that Sue praised Mary ]
We think [ that Sue speaks French ]

Smaller subordinate clauses: tense on verb but no that

We think [ Sue praised Mary ]

Smallest subordinate clauses: no that or tense on verb

I consider [ Sue to speak French well ]

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
General logic

Because language-technology AI systems are good at some things (e.g. analysing massive amounts of data very quickly), we expect them to be good at doing similar stuff when it comes to modelling/mimicking linguistic behaviour.
Because there are systematic gaps in the data, we expect language-technology AI systems to generally fare much worse when it comes modelling induction problems, broadly construed.



Is this what we see?


Yes and no.

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:

‘Nonlinguistic information’

i.e. which words are in the same class as which other words

Properly linguistic information

which words cooccur with which other words

in our parlance throughout this course, which heads must have complements and which ones do not have to?

title: Introduction to the science of language
section: Do LLMs have the same knowledge of language?
text:
Do LLMs have the same knowledge of language?
It’s complicated.

on the one hand, they demonstrate an impressive ability to generate text that has every hallmark of having been written by a human being

but does it know, for example, about the structure-sensitive rules of natural language?

it would appear so, at least to an extent


on the other hand, it reveals very profound and unexpected gaps that a human speaker would find quite shocking

title: Introduction to the science of language
section: Crucial curious little fact about English
text:
Crucial curious little fact about English

Questioning the subordinate clause subject is only possible if there is no that:

*Who do we think [ that __ praised Mary ]
Who do we think [ __ praised Mary ]

But questioning the subordinate clause object doesn’t care about that:

Who do we think [ that Sue praised __ ]
Who do we think [ Sue praised __ ]


Not restricted to English, that-like complementisers or wh-questions but a universal constraint with a well-defined set of exceptions, but English that-clauses will suffice for our purposes.

title: Introduction to the science of language
section: Is there really an induction problem here?
text:
Is there really an induction problem here?

There is: corpus studies of child-directed speech (and also adult-directed speech) show that the relevant data are almost never among the primary linguistic data to which a child is exposed

in a 11,308-utterance sample, only 2 utterances of that+object question and 0 utterances of that+subject question

as opposed to 159 that-less object questions and 13 that-less subject questions



Do LLMs know about these patterns?

title: Introduction to the science of language
text:
Some conclusions

we humans know something LLMs don’t despite having never been exposed to the data required to learn it
there may not even be such a thing as a ‘general learner’ at all (Chemla and Nefdt 2024)
even though the biases may not be in the data themselves, they can be introduced into the learner artificially, with better learning outcomes (Pearl and Sprouse 2013)
